newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan suspends private sugar, rice import duty.
newsitem.headline: Jordan suspends private sugar, rice import duty.

text.p: Jordan has suspended a 16-percent customs duty for a six-month trial period in an attempt to encourage private sugar and rice purchases, officials and traders said on Wednesday.

Officials at the Ministry of Supply, the state commodities buyer, said the cabinet decided on Tuesday to suspend the customs duty imposed two months ago when the government ended the public sector monopoly on grain imports.

Despite the August decision to open up imports which was part of a wider overhaul of a costly food subsidy programme, private traders have been reluctant to step in due to the duty which they said put them at a disadvantage versus state imports.
"Sugar imported by the ministry was totally exempt of customs... Now they realise that to encourage private sector purchases they should put traders on equal terms," said one trader.
But he said Tuesday's decision to lift the customs levy might not be enough in itself to lure private sector importers into the market.
"I doubt the private sector is geared to import sugar just now, with fluctuations in world prices, competition and the government continuing its traditional purchases," he said.
Jordan has been equally unsuccessful in prodding importers to purchase wheat, barley or corn, despite a lower five percent services tax on grain imports, traders say.
Only one grain importer, Yousef Nader Sons Company, has so far contracted 2,000 tonnes of Australian high quality rice to the local market and was supplying regular quantities.
"We want to prove to the government that we are capable of supplying the market," said Riad Talhami, manager at Yousef Nader Sons Company.
A small trial shipment of 3,000 tonnes of European sugar imported by the firm was arriving on Thursday and was expected to be a test of the government's intentions, traders said.

But most Jordanian importers have so far been just agents for international traders selling to the state. Analysts said they did not have storage or distribution facilities for large purchases and were wary of operating on their own.
Many grain traders believed deals were also being held back by uncertainty over government policy towards the private sector.
Few grain importers were willing to risk sizeable purchases from world markets until the rules were clarified, they said.
"There will be hesitancy and lack of decisiveness until the dust settles over the government's policy towards liberalisation of the private sector imports of grains," said another trader.
The government, sensing reluctance by the private sector to take on the market, was in the meantime maintaining normal grain purchases.
Once the private sector starts importing in large quantities it would start reducing its purchases, officials said.

Jordan recently bought 33,000 tonnes of U.S. medium grain rice along with 50,000 tonnes of U.S. corn for November shipment and has tendered to buy an extra 50,000 tonnes for December shipment on November 6.
A sugar tender for 30,000 tonnes was expected very soon.
